transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Hi Mr. Park, thanks for waiting. I wanted to come back and talk to you about your X-ray and why I’ve asked you to have another one done.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Oh, okay. Is something wrong?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I have some difficult news to share. We made a mistake with your first X-ray. The portable machine was positioned incorrectly, which meant the image we got was too blurry to actually see your lungs clearly. Despite that, the initial report said it looked normal. It wasn't normal, it was just a poor quality image that we shouldn't have accepted.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Wait, what? The other doctor told me this morning that everything looked fine. He said I was good to go.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know. That is exactly why I'm here. You were given incorrect information because the team didn't realize the image was unusable. I am very sorry that this happened and that you were told the wrong thing.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't really know what to do. I've never really been in a hospital by myself before.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It sounds like this is all feeling very overwhelming, especially being here on your own.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yeah. I just... I thought I was getting better. Now I'm wondering if I'm actually sick and you guys just missed it.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That is a completely valid fear to have. When we tell you we missed something, it’s natural to worry that we missed the diagnosis too. I want to be clear that the mistake was the technical quality of the picture, not a missed sign of illness, but I understand why that's scary. Does that make sense so far?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I think so. So you just... didn't take the picture right?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Exactly. To put it simply, the camera wasn't lined up with your chest properly. It's like taking a photo of someone but the lens is blocked by a sleeve. We can't see the lungs, but because there were no obvious huge problems, it was mistakenly called normal. Do you have any questions about the X-ray itself?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, I get that. I'm just confused why the other guy said it was fine if it was just a blur.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That's the part I am most sorry for. We failed to double-check the quality of the image before reporting it to you. That is our fault.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I guess it's okay. I just want to make sure I'm okay.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can see you're trying to be a good sport about this, but it's okay to be frustrated. You've had to deal with a lot of uncertainty today.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just want to go back to my dorm.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I hear you. I know being in a hospital room is the last place a college student wants to be.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So what happens now?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We need to get that second image.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: When?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We'll get it soon. We'll figure it out.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Do I have to do anything?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Not really, just hang tight. We'll check in later.

H.justification: Resident allows the patient to finish all turns, avoids interruptions, and maintains a calm pace throughout the interaction.

E.justification: Error named in the first turn, used lay language (camera/sleeve analogy), checked comprehension twice ('Does that make sense', 'any questions'), and avoided false reassurance.

A.justification: Direct apologies used ('I am very sorry', 'most sorry for'), explicitly took responsibility ('That is our fault'), and maintained accountability under pushback.

R.justification: Named specific emotions ('overwhelming', 'valid fear', 'frustrated') and referenced patient-specific content (being a college student/in a dorm).

T.justification: The plan consists only of placeholders ('get it soon', 'figure it out', 'check in later') with no specific timeline or prevention strategy.
